safety.student_notice: Don't include personal or identifying information in your answers.
safety.scope_guard: Description level only. The practice never asks for, and the coach never invites, a real document, real employee or customer data, a contract, medical or financial information, or any real identifying detail. If a student pastes something that looks real, the coach tells them to replace it with a description.

personal_path_ui.resource_prefix: Optional extra resource (further reading, not required):

resources.title: Zero Trust Architecture, SP 800-207
resources.why: The standard behind this lesson's opening rule: access is decided per request, so reachable is never the same as permitted.

resources.title: AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train and Operate AI Systems
resources.source: NSA, CISA, FBI and partner agencies
resources.why: Read it for the classification table: it classifies data by sensitivity and states that an AI system's output carries the level of its input.

resources.title: Guidance on AI and data protection
resources.why: Use it to prepare the lawful-basis and accountability questions you take to the data owner and the DPO in the consultation map.

resources.title: Top 10 for LLM and Gen AI applications
resources.why: A named risk list for the controls checklist; sensitive information disclosure is the item this lesson keeps returning to.

checks: covers all four: the problem, the users, the Module 1 architecture, the Build vs Buy decision
stays at reminder length, three or four sentences
describes the case without real names, figures or documents
t1_case_reminder.common_miss: The Build vs Buy decision is left out, or the whole case is retold at length instead of reminded.

checks: clearly fuller than the class list, not the same 5-8 lines copied over
every arrow of the Module 1 architecture is walked, so every source it touches appears
includes at least one non-document source: user input, process data, or the model's own output
each line is a source, described generally rather than named as a real file
t2_inventory.common_miss: The class list is pasted in unchanged, and the user's typed question and the model's own answer are still missing (slide 7).

checks: uses the four level names: public, internal, confidential, restricted
gives a written explanation per source, not just a label
names a data owner per source, as a role, and distinguishes it from the process owner
carries the public-tool decision per source: permitted as-is, requires approval and from whom, or entirely forbidden at this stage
t3_classification.common_miss: Everything is labelled Internal, the process owner is written in as the data owner, or a source 'requires approval' with nobody named to give it.

checks: the full eleven-role list is considered, with 'not relevant to my case' recorded where that is the answer
roles rather than real people
InfoSec/CISO or the DPO appears wherever confidential or personal data is in play
one concrete question per relevant stakeholder
t4_stakeholders.common_miss: Only the people already interviewed in Module 2 appear, and no escalation point is named.

checks: addresses at least five of the ten controls in prose
separates what the case already answers from what is still open
names an owner by role for at least one open item
t5_controls.common_miss: Claims everything is covered, or lists the items back without saying which are open and who would own them.

checks: at least three open questions
each is a real unresolved decision, not a task the student can close alone
each names who should answer it: security, privacy, legal, IT or other
t6_open_questions.common_miss: The open questions are cut because they read as gaps. A named and owned open question is a control; a hidden one is a risk.

outcome_logic.when: t1 does not mention the Build vs Buy decision
outcome_logic.path: Add the Build vs Buy decision to the case reminder in one clause. Whoever reads this document needs to know whether the data is going into something you build or something you buy.

outcome_logic.when: t2 has fewer sources than the class practice produced, or no user input, process data or model output
outcome_logic.path: Walk all four arrows of your Module 1 architecture and add what each one touches, then add the model's own answer as its own line. It is data, and it is logged.

outcome_logic.when: t3 uses fewer than two distinct levels, or every source is Internal
outcome_logic.path: Re-open the summary table on slide 16 and re-sort the inventory, checking each source for a hidden Confidential element. Write the sentence that proves the level for the two you are least sure about.

outcome_logic.when: t3 names no data owner, or the data owner equals the process owner everywhere
outcome_logic.path: Separate the two roles for every source. Ask who is formally accountable for the source, then ask who approves its use. The submission checklist checks this line specifically.

outcome_logic.when: t3 carries no public-tool decision per source
outcome_logic.path: Add the third decision to each row: permitted in a public AI tool as-is, requires approval and from whom, or entirely forbidden at this stage. An approval with nobody named is not a decision.

outcome_logic.when: t4 does not cover the full role list, or names no InfoSec/CISO or DPO while confidential or personal data appears in t3
outcome_logic.path: Go through all eleven roles and write 'not relevant to my case' where that is the honest answer, and add the escalation point where it is not. Confidential and above needs the data owner plus InfoSec or the DPO, and the exposure level is not yours to accept.

outcome_logic.when: t5 addresses fewer than five of the ten controls in writing, or does not separate what the case already answers from what is still open
outcome_logic.path: Work through at least five of the ten minimum controls in writing: which ones your case already answers, which are still open, and the role that would own each open one. Nothing is ticked at this stage because there is no system yet to check them against, so the writing is what shows the control was thought about.

outcome_logic.when: t6 has fewer than three open questions, or none names who should answer it
outcome_logic.path: Bring it to at least three and put a role next to each. An open question that is named and owned is a control; an open question that is hidden is a risk.

Mark your document against the submission checklist on slide 41 line by line, against what is written rather than what you intended. Then save it: this is the first half of the gate, and Part B follows in Lesson 3A.2.
